messages.subject: Re: rstan 2.7.0 is on CRAN !!!
parts:
On Monday, July 20, 2015 at 3:54:26 AM UTC-4, Sebastian Weber wrote:

Most of you know the good news already: rstan 2.7.0-1 is on CRAN servers! This will make installation of Stan so much easier.

It also makes crashing your R session so much easier, which is why we hadn't announced it previously. But it is being used in the Stan short course going on yesterday, today, and tomorrow. You still have to install a C++ compiler to actually estimate the parameters of a Stan program, but having the ability to do binary installs (particularly on Windows) is helpful if your computer / toolchain could not previously compile the Stan parser.

There are a lot of changes on the Stan side since 2.6.0, but Daniel will probably mention some of those sometime today. On the R side, the main two things are that it incorporates the ability to automatically save a bare version of a compiled model and to execute chains in parallel. Thus, you should not use the stan.R function from http://mc-stan.org.R anymore. When you do

library(rstan)

you will see the startup message

rstan (Version 2.7.0-1, packaged: , GitRev: 05c3d0058b6a)
For execution on a local, multicore CPU with excess RAM we recommend calling
rstan_options(auto_write = TRUE)
options(mc.cores = parallel::detectCores())

Doing

rstan_options(auto_write = TRUE)

means that a small foo.rda file will be saved in the same directory as foo.stan (or in tempdir() if that is not writable or you pass a Stan program in the form of a character string to stan()) when foo.stan is parsed into foo.cpp and compiled. Then, in the future, stan() will search the calling environment for the same stanmodel and if it doesn't find that will search for foo.rda on the hard disk or in tempdir(). If it finds such a foo.rda and some checks are passed (such as foo.stan has not been modified more recently or was parsed with an older version of rstan), then it will be loaded rather than recompiling foo.cpp. This approach was originally suggested by Sebastian.

However, it is easy to crash R this way and we have not been entirely successful at preventing all crashes. In particular, with that option enabled, if you pass non-existent data to stan(), it will compile then throw an error but not create an empty stanfit object. Then, when you fix the error, it won't find the non-existent stanfit object but will find foo.rda which will create two instances of the same DSO object in R's memory and crash R. Ironically, it is safer to not pass a list or environment of data to stan() because another feature is that stan() will automatically search the calling environment for objects whose names are the same as the objects in the data block of foo.stan and use those if it finds them. Thus, you can do something like

J <- 8
y <- c(28, 8, -3, 7, -1, 1, 18, 12)
sigma <- c(15, 10, 16, 11, 9, 11, 10, 18)
fit <- stan(file="8schools.stan")

and it will find matching objects named J, y, and sigma in both the data block of 8schools.stan and R's global environment.

If you have previously called

options(mc.cores = parallel::detectCores())

it will execute the chains in parallel (using the parLapply() function), utilizing (if necessary) as many cores as your computer has. This is only a problem if your computer does not have enough RAM to hold several copies of the data and the MCMC output simultaneously. You can also pass a cores argument to stan() or sampling() to override the mc.cores option. By default, cores is 1 and if you encounter a runtime error, you should call stan() again with cores = 1 to possibly see a better version of the error message before posting on stan-users.

If you are not using RStudio but instead using the R GUI for Windows or Mac (there is something seriously wrong with you but whatever) calling stan() in parallel will by default open a web browser on a temporary file that you can refresh to see the progress of the chains. This can be annoying for chains that execute very quickly and can be prevented by specifying open_progress = FALSE in the call to stan() or sampling(). This should not be an issue if you are using RStudio or a terminal, in which case the output will be piped to the console. Users of knitr will like this better because it the progress is not captured in the processed file. The most recent version of RStudio also has basic support for .stan files and a "Check" button you can press to see if the active .stan file parses. If anyone knows how to make RStudio do code completion on .stan files in the future, let us know.

There is no set_cppo() function anymore (or rather there is but it doesn't do anything but throw a warning), which I have seen a lot of people using in .R scripts (which was inappropriate even when the function did stuff). If you need to change the optimization level or other settings, you have to edit your personal .Makevars file yourself, see

https://github.com/stan-dev/rstan/wiki/RStan-Getting-Started#configuration

Basically, it should be fine with -O2 but executes slightly faster with -O3.

If you are installing rstan from source using g++ version 4.9.x or later, definitely specify a CXXFLAGS that does not include the -g flag or does include -flto -ffat-lto-objects; otherwise, the Stan parser will take up 250+ Mb of space on your disk. This shouldn't be a problem if you install the binary version of the rstan package from CRAN (which is typical for Windows and recent Macs).

The expose_stan_functions() R function --- which was formerly referred to as testify() --- allows you to test that your user-defined Stan functions are working correctly by calling them in R and comparing them to the results of other R functions that are known to be correct. This is, e.g. how I figured out Phillip's problem described here

https://groups.google.com/d/msg/stan-users/ErUE-Z25sec/ScHiTmtI_GYJ

So, if you are not utilizing user-defined Stan functions for all non-trivial operations in your .stan file and / or not validating those user-defined Stan functions in R before you call stan(), you are doing it wrong. User-defined Stan functions can also do random number generation, and thus can be used to draw from a posterior predictive distribution after stan() is done or to even do simulations that are not connected to any Stan program.

We see a lot of posts on stan-users about Stan programs that do not sample well, but we do not see a lot of corresponding pairs() plots. You should have been using the pairs() function already, but its defaults have been improved for rstan 2.7.0. Now, it splits the lower and upper triangles at the median accept_stat__ and overplots points if the Markov Chain diverges on that iteration (in red) or exceeds the maximum treedepth (in yellow). This gives you a sense of what parameter interaction causes these sampling difficulties and whether it is a problem of the Markov Chain(s) getting stuck in the tail or being unable to navigate around the mode. The pairs() function takes a pars argument that you should use to specify which parameters to plot. By default, it does all the parameters which is often unreadable (and slow). You should definitely be looking at lp__ and things like variance parameters and other hyperparameters.

Any function that takes a pars argument (like stan, plot, traceplot, and print.stanfit) now has an include argument that defaults to TRUE. This means that any parameter(s) specified by the pars argument is / are included by that function. If include = FALSE, then any parameter(s) specified by the pars argument is / are excluded by that function. So, if you have a lot of named parameters but only a small number that you want to omit, then you can name them with the pars argument and specify include = FALSE. This is particularly useful for stan() if you have latent variables that you do not want to store MCMC samples of (because there are so many of them) but you still want to see the posterior means of those latent variables by subsequently calling get_posterior_mean(). See

https://groups.google.com/d/msg/stan-users/t2B2W_AjlDc/GvwlKi3fk1QJ

There is also a new lookup() function in RStan that inputs an R function or a name of an R function and returns the corresponding Stan function (if it finds one). For example,

> lookup(chol)
         StanFunction  Arguments ReturnType Page
72 cholesky_decompose (matrix A)     matrix  331

Page refers to the page of the current Stan User's Manual where the cholesky_decompose function is defined. If you pass it "~", it returns all sampling statements defined in the Stan language. Otherwise, if it fails to find a Stan function, it interprets the input as a regexp and returns matching Stan functions.

There is probably a bunch more stuff that I don't remember now since I haven't been using rstan 2.6.0 personally or for my class. You should definitely upgrade to 2.7.0-1 but be very careful about passing the correct data to Stan until we can upload a 2.7.0-2. If you are maintaining a non-CRAN R package that relies on rstan or a CRAN package that unofficially relies on rstan, let us know by posting on stan-users or emailing. Otherwise, we won't know whether changes to rstan breaks something.

Ben

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: rstan 2.7.0 is on CRAN !!!
parts:
This is a big release. We've been saving the official announcement until
PyStan is ready. Here are the release notes (and we've added another
developer, Dustin Tran, since then).

Below are the release notes for Stan C++. CmdStan has variational
inference, but I don't think there's an R interface for variational
inference in 2.7.0. We should have that interface worked out very soon
and will be releasing a 2.7.0.2 version of RStan or a 2.7.1 version
of Stan and RStan.

- Bob


v2.7.0 (9 July 2015)
======================================================================

New Team Members
--------------------------------------------------
* Alp Kucukelbir, who brings you variational inference
* Robert L. Grant, who brings you the StataStan interface

Major New Feature
--------------------------------------------------
* Black-box variational inference, mean field and full
rank (#1505)

New Features
--------------------------------------------------
* Line numbers reported for runtime errors (#1195)
* Wiener first passage time density (#765) (thanks to
Michael Schvartsman)
* Partial initialization (#1069)
* NegBinomial2 RNG (#1471) and PoissonLog RNG (#1458) and extended
range for Dirichlet RNG (#1474) and fixed Poisson RNG for older
Mac compilers (#1472)
* Error messages now use operator notation (#1401)
* More specific error messages for illegal assignments (#1100)
* More specific error messages for illegal sampling statement
signatures (#1425)
* Extended range on ibeta derivatives with wide impact on CDFs (#1426)
* Display initialization error messages (#1403)
* Works with Intel compilers and GCC 4.4 (#1506, #1514, #1519)

Bug Fixes
--------------------------------------------------
* Allow functions ending in _lp to call functions ending in _lp (#1500)
* Update warnings to catch uses of illegal sampling functions like
CDFs and updated declared signatures (#1152)
* Disallow constraints on local variables (#1295)
* Allow min() and max() in variable declaration bounds and remove
unnecessary use of math.h and top-level :: namespace (#1436)
* Updated exponential lower bound check (#1179)
* Extended sum to work with zero size arrays (#1443)
* Positive definiteness checks fixed (were > 1e-8, now > 0) (#1386)

Code Reorganization and Back End Upgrades
--------------------------------------------------
* New static constants (#469, #765)
* Added major/minor/patch versions as properties (#1383)
* Pulled all math-like functionality into stan::math namespace
* Pulled the Stan Math Library out into its own repository (#1520)
* Included in Stan C++ repository as submodule
* Removed final usage of std::cout and std::cerr (#699) and
updated tests for null streams (#1239)
* Removed over 1000 CppLint warnings
* Remove model write CSV methods (#445)
* Reduced generality of operators in fvar (#1198)
* Removed folder-level includes due to order issues (part of Math
reorg) and include math.hpp include (#1438)
* Updated to Boost 1.58 (#1457)
* Travis continuous integration for Linux (#607)
* Add grad() method to math::var for autodiff to encapsulate math::vari
* Added finite diff functionals for testing (#1271)
* More configurable distribution unit tests (#1268)
* Clean up directory-level includes (#1511)
* Removed all lint from new math lib and add cpplint to build lib
(#1412)
* Split out derivative functionals (#1389)


Manual and Dcoumentation
--------------------------------------------------
* New Logo in Manual; remove old logos (#1023)
* Corrected all known bug reports and typos; details in
issues #1420, #1508, #1496
* Thanks to Sunil Nandihalli, Andy Choi, Sebastian Weber,
Heraa Hu, @jonathan-g (GitHub handle), M. B. Joseph, Damjan
Vukcevic, @tosh1ki (GitHub handle), Juan S. Casallas
* Fix some parsing issues for index (#1498)
* Added chapter on variational inference
* Added strangely unrelated regressions and multivariate probit
examples
* Discussion from Ben Goodrich about reject() and sampling
* Start to reorganize code with fast examples first, then
explanations
* Added CONTRIBUTING.md file (#1408)

parts:
Thanks for rstan 2.7.0-1. Great work.

You encouraged use of pairs() following stanfit. The following suggestion might make pairs.stanfit more useable. 

I tried requesting a log scale for the 8schools.stan example for the tau parameter. Tau is bunched up right next to 0, and a log(tau) plot would spread it out better. The base "pairs" function has an example specifying the log scale for the first four variables in the iris data set with pairs(iris, log=1:4), but pairs(fit, log=2, pars=c("mu","tau","lp__")) doesn't work with fit from the 8schools.stan example. I've searched "pairs" and "log scale" on stan-user google groups to no avail. While it's simple to create a transformed xx = log(tau) variable and have graphical plots of xx, often the interpretation or familiarity is on the original tau scale. And the log scale plots are usually closer to symmetrical than the original scale.

More generally, I would like to request a log scale option for traceplot, pairs, and other stan graphics. And would it be possible to have the log scale as the default for scale parameters (sigma's), since they naturally have a log scale (e.g. distance scale - mm, cm, m, km etc)? I'm not sure how feasible it is for stan to recognize automatically a scale parameter though. Finally, back to the pairs(fit) example, having a -2 Log Likelihood variable = -2 * (L - L_max) in addition to lp__ would be helpful.

Thank you!
